newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Corporate deals coming.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Corporate deals coming.

text.p: Asian debt markets were quiet on Friday but a couple of corporate issues are set for launch next week.
Peregrine Fixed Income is finishing up the roadshow for a US$100 million floating rate note issue for Indonesian conglomerate Dharmala Inti Utama.
The notes have a final maturity of three years but can be put on the second anniversary. They are expected to price at 99.00.
The exact coupon rate has not been decided, but it is expected to be set at 250 to 300 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate.
"On the face of it, the deal looks alright for high-yield investors that are interested in floating rate paper," remarked one syndicate manager.

Dharmala Inti Utama is the holding company of Indonesia's Dharmala group, which controls six companies trading on the Jakarta Stock Exchange and 25 non-public companies. Its interests include agri-food, financial services, real estate, electronics and packaging and consumer/retail businesses.
China's Tingyi Noodles will make its presentation to Hong Kong bankers on Monday and other Asian cities will follow.
The company is planning what bankers say is its first floating rate note issue. The US$150 million FRN has a maturity of three years. ING Barings is the lead.
Taiwan-owned, China-based and Hong Kong-listed Tingyi is one of China's biggest manufacturers of instant noodles.
It posted a 58 percent rise in sales in the first six months of 1996 but its profit margin was slightly lower than last year, the company's managing director was quoted as saying earlier this week.
Tingyi will post its interim results on September 9, the same day as the Hong Kong roadshow for its FRN.
"It should be a good deal," said one banker. "It's a good company, it has a good story to tell and it's got a good operation. I think from a bank's perspective the deal will go quite well," he said.
Because the instant noodlemaker is based primarily in China's Tianjin, the deal will be seen as having China risk despite the Hong Kong listing and Taiwan management, he added.
Bankers said trading in Asian debt instruments was slow this week, with traders jittery ahead of Friday's U.S. payrolls data.

Economists polled by Reuters forecast a 244,000 gain in U.S. non-farm payrolls in August after a 193,000 rise in July. They see average hourly earnings rising 0.3 percent after a 0.2 percent fall the prior month.

A sharp rise in new jobs could spur renewed speculation of a near-term tightening by the Federal Reserve. In U.S. trade Thursday, Treasuries slumped, partly on news U.S. jobless claims fell a surprise 15,000 in the week ended August 31.
The long bond ended down 20/32 point to yield 7.15 percent.
"People are feeling pretty defensive this week," remarked a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank in Hong Kong.
